subtopic_detail: Suppressive therapy for recurrent bacterial vaginosis
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29 year old woman who has had four episodes of a thin grey discharge with a strong fishy smell in the past twelve months. Each episode has settled completely with a week of treatment and then returned within six to eight weeks, and she says the smell is worse after sex and after her period.

She is in a stable relationship with one male partner, uses condoms inconsistently and does not douche. There is no itch, no soreness and no pain with sex. Vaginal pH today is 5.2, microscopy shows clue cells with an absence of lactobacilli, and there is no candidal pseudohyphae. Nucleic acid testing is negative for Trichomonas vaginalis, chlamydia and gonorrhoea.

data_table.Examination: Thin homogeneous grey discharge coating the vaginal walls, no vulval erythema, cervix normal
data_table.Investigations: Vaginal pH 5.2; clue cells present with absent lactobacilli; nucleic acid testing negative for trichomonas, chlamydia and gonorrhoea

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give a single 2 g oral metronidazole dose and review as needed
options.rationale: Single dose therapy has a higher relapse rate than a seven day course and does nothing to address a pattern of recurrence already established over a year (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Prescribe a seven day course of oral fluconazole weekly for six months
options.rationale: Weekly fluconazole is the suppressive regimen for recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis, and the pH of 5.2 with clue cells and no pseudohyphae excludes that diagnosis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Treat with oral metronidazole then twice weekly intravaginal gel
options.rationale: Recurrent disease is treated with a standard induction course followed by intravaginal metronidazole gel twice weekly for four to six months, which substantially reduces recurrence while suppression continues (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Australasian Sexual Health Alliance STI Management Guidelines).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
Australasian Sexual Health Alliance STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Prescribe oral clindamycin and treat her regular male sexual partner
options.rationale: Clindamycin is the alternative agent for allergy or intolerance rather than a first choice, and partner treatment is not part of standard Australian guidance for this condition (Source: Australasian Sexual Health Alliance STI Management Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Sexual Health Alliance STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Advise vaginal douching with a lactic acid preparation each week
options.rationale: Douching disrupts the vaginal flora further and is an independent risk factor for the condition rather than a treatment for it (Source: Australasian Sexual Health Alliance STI Management Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Sexual Health Alliance STI Management Guidelines

explanation.summary: Bacterial vaginosis reflects loss of lactobacilli and overgrowth of anaerobes forming a polymicrobial biofilm, which explains why single courses of antibiotics so often fail to hold. Diagnosis rests on the Amsel criteria of thin homogeneous discharge, pH above 4.5, clue cells and a positive amine test, of which three are required. Recurrence affects more than half of women within twelve months, and suppressive intravaginal therapy after induction is the intervention with the best evidence. Treatment matters beyond symptoms because the condition increases susceptibility to sexually transmitted infections and is associated with preterm birth in pregnancy.
key_points: Diagnosis requires three of the four Amsel criteria
A vaginal pH above 4.5 argues against candidiasis
Induction therapy followed by twice weekly intravaginal gel reduces recurrence
Douching is a risk factor and never a treatment
Routine male partner treatment is not part of Australian guidance
explanation.pearls: Warn women taking oral metronidazole to avoid alcohol during the course and for 24 hours afterwards because of the disulfiram like reaction, and note that intravaginal gel avoids this problem during months of suppression.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
Australasian Sexual Health Alliance STI Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Time critical investigation after intrauterine foetal death at 34 weeks
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar caring for a 32 year old woman in her first pregnancy who presented at 34 weeks and 2 days because she had not felt the baby move for two days. Ultrasound has confirmed the absence of foetal cardiac activity and you have broken this news with the midwife present.

She has had no bleeding, no abdominal pain and no rupture of membranes. Her blood pressure has been normal at every visit and is normal now, her urine shows no protein and she has no headache or visual disturbance. Her booking bloods were unremarkable and she is rhesus D positive. Induction of labour is planned to begin later today after she has had time with her family.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88, blood pressure 116/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 31 cm, uterus soft and non tender, no vaginal bleeding
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound confirms absent foetal cardiac activity; urinalysis shows no protein; full blood count and liver function within normal limits

lead_in: Which investigation is most important to obtain before the birth?

options.text: Arrange a thrombophilia screen including lupus anticoagulant now
options.rationale: Acute phase changes and pregnancy itself distort thrombophilia results, so antiphospholipid testing is deferred and repeated at least twelve weeks later if indicated (Source: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death).
source_refs: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death

options.text: Send maternal blood for a full torch serology panel before the birth
options.rationale: Untargeted torch serology has a very low diagnostic yield in stillbirth and has been removed from routine protocols in favour of placental histopathology and directed testing (Source: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death).
source_refs: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death

options.text: Arrange a whole body magnetic resonance imaging scan of the foetus
options.rationale: Imaging is offered as an adjunct or alternative when parents decline autopsy, and it is arranged after the birth rather than being the priority beforehand (Source: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death).
source_refs: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death

options.text: Perform amniocentesis for karyotype after the birth has occurred
options.rationale: Genetic material is obtained from placental or foetal tissue at delivery, and amniocentesis after the birth is not a procedure that exists (Source: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death).
source_refs: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death

options.text: Take maternal blood for a Kleihauer test before birth is induced
options.rationale: Massive fetomaternal haemorrhage is a recognised and otherwise silent cause, and the Kleihauer must be taken before labour because the transplacental passage of cells during birth invalidates the result (Source: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death; RANZCOG guidance on stillbirth investigation).
source_refs: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death
RANZCOG guidance on stillbirth investigation

explanation.summary: Stillbirth affects around one in every 130 Australian births and up to a third remain unexplained after investigation, so a systematic protocol matters both for future pregnancy planning and for the family's understanding. The Perinatal Society of Australia and New Zealand core investigation set includes placental histopathology, autopsy offered to every family, foetal and placental genetic testing, a Kleihauer, maternal glucose and thyroid testing and a full blood count. The Kleihauer is unique in that its timing is critical, because labour and birth themselves cause fetomaternal transfusion and destroy the interpretability of a later sample. Placental histopathology has the highest single test yield and is never declined on the family's behalf.
key_points: Take the Kleihauer before labour begins because birth invalidates the result
Placental histopathology has the highest diagnostic yield of any single test
Autopsy is offered to every family and consent is sought sensitively
Untargeted torch serology is no longer part of the core investigation set
Thrombophilia and antiphospholipid testing is deferred to at least twelve weeks postpartum
explanation.pearls: A Kleihauer showing more than about 20 mL of foetal blood in the maternal circulation identifies massive fetomaternal haemorrhage as the cause, and this diagnosis is otherwise entirely silent because the mother has no pain, bleeding or abnormal observations.

sources.label: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death
RANZCOG guidance on stillbirth investigation

subtopic_detail: Referral pathway for a suspicious adnexal mass after menopause
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 63 year old woman who has had three months of persistent bloating, a feeling of fullness after only a few mouthfuls and needing to pass urine more often. She has attributed all of this to getting older and to a change in her diet.

She went through menopause at 51 years, has never used hormone therapy and has no family history of breast or ovarian cancer. Her weight is stable and she has had no vaginal bleeding. A pelvic ultrasound performed yesterday describes a 7 cm right adnexal mass with solid areas and papillary projections, together with a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her CA125 result is back today.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen mildly distended, no palpable mass, no lymphadenopathy, no ascitic shifting dullness
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic ultrasound shows a 7 cm right adnexal mass with solid areas and papillary projections and free pelvic fluid; CA125 210 kU/L (less than 35)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a gynaecological oncology centre for definitive surgery
options.rationale: A high risk of malignancy index driven by postmenopausal status, a complex mass with solid areas and a raised CA125 mandates referral to a specialist centre, where survival is measurably better with complete cytoreduction (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines; RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines
RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass

options.text: Repeat the pelvic ultrasound and the CA125 in three months time
options.rationale: Interval surveillance is for simple unilocular cysts under 5 cm with a normal marker, and delaying a complex mass with ascites allows the disease to advance a stage (Source: RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass

options.text: Arrange ultrasound guided aspiration of the cyst fluid for cytology
options.rationale: Aspiration risks spilling malignant cells into the peritoneum and upstaging the disease, and a negative cytology result would not exclude cancer (Source: RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass

options.text: Book a laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy at the local district hospital
options.rationale: Cystectomy in a general unit risks intraoperative rupture and incomplete staging, both of which worsen outcome compared with primary surgery in a specialist centre (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Start a trial of hormone therapy and reassess the symptoms after that
options.rationale: Bloating and early satiety here reflect a pelvic mass rather than oestrogen deficiency, and a therapeutic trial would waste weeks without addressing the finding on imaging (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

explanation.summary: Ovarian cancer has no effective population screening test, so it is detected by acting on the vague but persistent symptom cluster of bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency and abdominal pain in women over 50. The risk of malignancy index combines menopausal status, ultrasound morphology features and the CA125 level, and a score above 200 identifies women who should have primary surgery in a gynaecological oncology unit. Centralised surgery matters because the survival benefit comes from complete macroscopic cytoreduction, which needs bowel and upper abdominal expertise available in the same theatre. CA125 is unreliable in premenopausal women because endometriosis, fibroids, pelvic inflammatory disease and even menstruation raise it.
key_points: Persistent bloating and early satiety in a woman over 50 warrant pelvic ultrasound and CA125
The risk of malignancy index combines menopausal status, ultrasound features and CA125
Complex masses with solid areas or ascites are referred to a specialist centre
Cyst aspiration risks peritoneal spill and upstaging
CA125 lacks specificity in premenopausal women
explanation.pearls: In a woman under 40 with a solid ovarian mass, request alpha fetoprotein, beta human chorionic gonadotrophin and lactate dehydrogenase rather than relying on CA125, because germ cell tumours are the dominant histology in that age group.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines
RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass

subtopic_detail: Whether urodynamic testing is required before continence surgery
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 57 year old woman who has leaked urine for two years whenever she coughs, sneezes or lifts her grandchildren. She has completed six months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training with a continence physiotherapist and says it has made no difference to her leaking.

She describes no sudden desperate need to pass urine, gets up once at night and empties her bladder without straining or hesitancy. A three day bladder diary records normal voided volumes with no urgency episodes. Her cough stress test is positive with immediate leakage, her post void residual volume is 30 mL, and there is no prolapse below the level of the hymen. Urinalysis shows no blood, protein, nitrites or leucocytes.

data_table.Examination: Positive cough stress test with immediate leakage, no prolapse beyond the hymen, good pelvic floor contraction
data_table.Investigations: Post void residual 30 mL; three day bladder diary shows normal volumes without urgency; urinalysis clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform multichannel urodynamic testing before any continence surgery
options.rationale: Randomised evidence shows that preoperative urodynamics does not improve outcomes in women with uncomplicated demonstrable stress incontinence, so it adds cost and discomfort without changing the plan (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women; VALUE randomised trial).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women
VALUE randomised trial

options.text: Start oxybutynin and reassess her symptoms again in three months
options.rationale: Antimuscarinics treat urgency and urge incontinence, and her diary and history document neither, so it would produce dry mouth and constipation without benefit (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women

options.text: Repeat another six months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training
options.rationale: A properly supervised programme has already been completed without benefit, and repeating it delays definitive treatment for a symptom that is limiting her activity (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women

options.text: Refer for a midurethral sling without further urodynamic testing
options.rationale: Uncomplicated stress incontinence with a positive cough stress test, normal emptying, no urgency and no significant prolapse can proceed straight to surgery, and omitting urodynamics does not worsen results (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women; VALUE randomised trial).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women
VALUE randomised trial

options.text: Arrange cystoscopy and a bladder diary before proceeding any further
options.rationale: Cystoscopy is indicated for haematuria, recurrent infection, pain or suspected fistula, and the bladder diary has already been completed (Source: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women

explanation.summary: Stress urinary incontinence is diagnosed clinically when leakage is demonstrated with a cough in a woman describing effort related loss, and supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months is universally first line. Urodynamics was traditionally mandatory before surgery, but randomised evidence established that office evaluation alone gives equivalent outcomes in the uncomplicated case. Testing retains a clear role when the picture is mixed or discordant, when emptying is impaired, after failed previous continence surgery, or where significant prolapse may be masking incontinence. Women considering a midurethral sling must be counselled about mesh specific risks and about the availability of autologous fascial sling and colposuspension.
key_points: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months precedes surgery
A positive cough stress test with normal emptying defines uncomplicated stress incontinence
Urodynamics is not required before surgery in the uncomplicated case
Testing is indicated for mixed symptoms, voiding dysfunction, prior surgery or significant prolapse
Mesh specific risks and non mesh alternatives must be discussed before a sling
explanation.pearls: A post void residual above 100 mL changes the pathway entirely, because a sling placed in a woman who empties poorly can precipitate retention requiring intermittent self catheterisation or tape division.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Urinary Incontinence in Women
VALUE randomised trial

subtopic_detail: Decompensating rheumatic mitral stenosis in the second trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 29 year old woman at 24 weeks gestation who has become breathless walking up the single flight of stairs to her flat over the past three weeks. Last night she woke suddenly needing to sit on the edge of the bed to catch her breath.

She grew up in Vanuatu and moved to Australia at 19 years, and had several episodes of sore joints and fever as a child. She has no chest pain, no cough and no fever, and her chest is clear on auscultation with no wheeze. Her jugular venous pressure is 4 cm and there is no ankle swelling beyond what is usual for her gestation. On auscultation there is a loud first heart sound with an opening snap and a rumbling mid diastolic murmur at the apex, and an echocardiogram today reports a mitral valve area of 1.2 cm2 with a mean gradient of 12 mmHg and normal left ventricular function.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 and regular, blood pressure 104/68, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8, foetal heart rate 146
data_table.Examination: Loud first heart sound with opening snap and apical mid diastolic murmur, chest clear, jugular venous pressure 4 cm
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram shows mitral valve area 1.2 cm2, mean gradient 12 mmHg, normal left ventricular systolic function, sinus rhythm on electrocardiogram

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Start an intravenous frusemide infusion and aim for negative balance
options.rationale: Aggressive diuresis in a preload dependent stenotic lesion drops cardiac output and uteroplacental perfusion, and her clear chest and jugular venous pressure of 4 cm show she is not congested (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Start metoprolol to lengthen diastolic filling and limit her activity
options.rationale: Symptoms in mitral stenosis are driven by the tachycardia of pregnancy shortening diastole, so rate control with a beta blocker plus activity restriction is the first line intervention and improves the transvalvular gradient directly (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy; ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy
ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Arrange delivery by caesarean section within the next 48 hours
options.rationale: Delivery at 24 weeks carries extreme prematurity risk and the haemodynamic stress of surgery, and medical optimisation almost always allows the pregnancy to continue for many weeks (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Start nifedipine to reduce afterload and improve exercise capacity
options.rationale: Afterload reduction helps regurgitant lesions but not a fixed stenosis, and the resulting reflex tachycardia would shorten diastolic filling and worsen her symptoms (Source: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy).
source_refs: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Start therapeutic enoxaparin and arrange balloon valvuloplasty now
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is indicated for atrial fibrillation or thrombus, and she is in sinus rhythm, while valvuloplasty is reserved for symptoms that persist despite maximal medical therapy (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Rheumatic mitral stenosis is the cardiac lesion most likely to decompensate in pregnancy because the fifty per cent rise in cardiac output and the physiological tachycardia both increase flow across a fixed orifice while shortening the time available for it. Symptoms typically appear in the second trimester as the haemodynamic load peaks, and a valve area below 1.5 cm2 marks moderate stenosis with a high likelihood of deterioration. Beta blockade is counterintuitive to students used to treating breathlessness with diuretics, but lengthening diastole is the mechanism that lowers left atrial pressure here. Anticoagulation becomes mandatory if atrial fibrillation develops, and percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty is the intervention of choice when medical therapy fails, ideally after 20 weeks with abdominal shielding.
key_points: Mitral stenosis decompensates as cardiac output peaks in the second trimester
Tachycardia shortens diastole and is the main driver of symptoms
Beta blockade with activity restriction is first line therapy
Diuretics are used cautiously and only for genuine pulmonary congestion
Balloon valvuloplasty is reserved for failure of medical therapy
explanation.pearls: New atrial fibrillation in pregnant mitral stenosis is a medical emergency requiring immediate rate control and therapeutic anticoagulation, because loss of the atrial contribution to filling can precipitate pulmonary oedema within hours.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy
ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation choice for a mechanical heart valve in early pregnancy
stem:
You are the obstetric medicine registrar seeing a 31 year old woman who has just found out she is 5 weeks pregnant. She has a bileaflet mechanical aortic valve replacement performed six years ago for congenital bicuspid disease and has had no thromboembolic events since.

She takes warfarin 3.5 mg daily and her international normalised ratio has been stable within target for the last year, including a result of 2.8 taken last week. She has no atrial fibrillation, no left ventricular impairment and her most recent echocardiogram showed normal prosthetic valve gradients. She has heard that her medication can harm the baby and is anxious about what to do.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 112/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Crisp mechanical second heart sound, no murmur of regurgitation, no signs of heart failure
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 2.8 (target 2.0-3.0); echocardiogram shows normal prosthetic gradients and normal left ventricular function

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan?

options.text: Change to therapeutic enoxaparin twice daily for the first trimester
options.rationale: Low molecular weight heparin avoids embryopathy but carries the highest rate of valve thrombosis of the available strategies, so it is chosen when the warfarin dose exceeds 5 mg daily or the woman declines warfarin after counselling (Source: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy; RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy).
source_refs: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Change to a direct oral anticoagulant for the whole of the pregnancy
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves at any time because of excess thrombosis and bleeding, and they are additionally not recommended in pregnancy (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Stop anticoagulation until 12 weeks and use aspirin in the meantime
options.rationale: Antiplatelet therapy alone provides no protection against mechanical valve thrombosis, and interrupting anticoagulation risks a catastrophic and often fatal event (Source: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy).
source_refs: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Change to unfractionated heparin by infusion until 12 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Unfractionated heparin requires hospitalisation with frequent monitoring and carries heparin induced thrombocytopenia and osteoporosis risk, so it is reserved for the peripartum period rather than the whole first trimester (Source: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Continue warfarin now and change to heparin at 36 weeks gestation
options.rationale: Embryopathy risk is dose related and is under three per cent when the daily requirement is 5 mg or less, so continuing warfarin gives the lowest maternal thrombotic risk, with conversion to heparin near term to allow safe delivery (Source: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy; RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy).
source_refs: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pregnancy with a mechanical valve presents an unavoidable conflict between maternal thrombotic risk and foetal teratogenicity, and no strategy eliminates both. Warfarin gives the lowest rate of valve thrombosis but crosses the placenta and causes a characteristic embryopathy with nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses when used between 6 and 12 weeks. That risk is strongly dose dependent, and a requirement of 5 mg or less daily brings it to a level where continuation through the first trimester is the recommended course after full counselling. Warfarin is always converted to heparin from around 36 weeks because a fully anticoagulated foetus cannot safely negotiate labour and is at risk of intracranial haemorrhage.
key_points: Warfarin embryopathy risk is dose dependent and low at 5 mg daily or less
The teratogenic window is approximately 6 to 12 weeks gestation
Low molecular weight heparin carries the highest valve thrombosis risk of the options
Direct oral anticoagulants are contraindicated with mechanical valves
Convert to heparin around 36 weeks to allow safe delivery
explanation.pearls: If low molecular weight heparin is used with a mechanical valve, anti Xa levels must be measured with a peak target of about 1.0 to 1.2 units per mL four hours after the dose, because fixed weight based dosing alone is associated with valve thrombosis.

sources.label: ESC Guidelines on Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Cardiac Disease in Pregnancy
Australian Medicines Handbook

subtopic_detail: Surveillance plan in the pregnancy after a placentally mediated stillbirth
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar seeing a 30 year old woman at 12 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first baby was stillborn at 36 weeks two years ago after she noticed reduced movements, and the placental histopathology reported extensive maternal vascular malperfusion with accelerated villous maturation and infarction. The birth weight was on the 4th centile.

She has a body mass index of 24 kg/m2, has never smoked and has no diabetes, hypertension or autoimmune disease. Antiphospholipid antibodies were negative on two occasions at least twelve weeks apart. Her blood pressure today is normal, her urine has no protein and her dating scan is consistent with her last menstrual period.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76, blood pressure 110/68, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24 kg/m2, uterus consistent with dates, no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Antiphospholipid antibodies negative on two occasions twelve weeks apart; dating ultrasound consistent; urinalysis shows no protein

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for this pregnancy?

options.text: Start prophylactic enoxaparin from now until six weeks postpartum
options.rationale: Randomised trials of heparin for placentally mediated complications have not shown a reduction in recurrent stillbirth or growth restriction in women without thrombophilia (Source: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death).
source_refs: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death

options.text: Begin weekly cardiotocography from 28 weeks and expect a term birth
options.rationale: Cardiotocography assesses foetal wellbeing at a single moment and does not predict stillbirth days later, so it cannot substitute for growth surveillance and planned timing of birth (Source: RANZCOG: Timing of Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Timing of Birth

options.text: Start low dose aspirin before 16 weeks with serial growth scans
options.rationale: Maternal vascular malperfusion identifies a placental phenotype that recurs, and aspirin started before 16 weeks reduces preterm pre eclampsia and growth restriction while serial third trimester growth and Doppler surveillance guides the timing of birth (Source: RANZCOG: Pre eclampsia and Hypertension in Pregnancy; PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pre eclampsia and Hypertension in Pregnancy
PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death

options.text: Plan elective birth at 37 weeks without any additional surveillance
options.rationale: Planned earlier birth is part of the strategy, but committing to a date without growth surveillance misses the growth restricted foetus who needs to be born sooner (Source: RANZCOG: Timing of Birth).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Timing of Birth

options.text: Reassure that recurrence is not increased and provide routine care
options.rationale: A previous stillbirth roughly doubles the risk in the next pregnancy, and a documented placental cause raises it further, so routine care understates the risk (Source: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death).
source_refs: PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death

explanation.summary: The pregnancy after a stillbirth carries both a measurably increased recurrence risk and a very high level of parental anxiety, and both need an explicit plan made early. A documented placental cause is actually useful information because maternal vascular malperfusion behaves like the placental disease spectrum that includes pre eclampsia and growth restriction, which has a proven preventive intervention. Aspirin must be started before 16 weeks to influence trophoblast invasion, and the Australian dose used in this context is 100 to 150 mg at night. Surveillance then focuses on serial growth with umbilical artery Doppler from the late second trimester, with birth usually planned between 37 and 39 weeks and earlier if growth falters.
key_points: Previous stillbirth approximately doubles the risk in a subsequent pregnancy
Maternal vascular malperfusion places the pregnancy on the placental disease spectrum
Aspirin must begin before 16 weeks to be effective
Serial growth scans with umbilical artery Doppler guide timing of birth
Heparin has not been shown to prevent recurrent placentally mediated stillbirth
explanation.pearls: Aspirin for placental prophylaxis is given at 100 to 150 mg at night rather than in the morning, because evening dosing produces a greater reduction in preterm pre eclampsia in randomised comparison.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Pre eclampsia and Hypertension in Pregnancy
PSANZ Clinical Practice Guideline for Care Around Stillbirth and Neonatal Death
RANZCOG: Timing of Birth

subtopic_detail: Seizure at 33 weeks in a woman with pre existing epilepsy
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called to the assessment unit for a 24 year old woman at 33 weeks gestation. Her partner witnessed a generalised tonic clonic seizure lasting about ninety seconds at home, with tongue biting and a period of confusion afterwards. She has known generalised epilepsy and takes lamotrigine, and this is her first seizure in two years.

She has no headache, no visual disturbance and no epigastric pain, and her partner says she has had no swelling of her face or hands. She is now fully alert and orientated. Her reflexes are normal without clonus, and the cardiotocograph shows a normal baseline with accelerations and no decelerations. A lamotrigine level taken on arrival has come back well below her usual pre pregnancy value.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96, blood pressure 148/94, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9, foetal heart rate baseline 140
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, no clonus, normal fundi, no facial or hand oedema, tongue laceration present
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio 12 mg/mmol (less than 30); platelets 240 x10^9/L (150-400); alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L (less than 35); creatinine 58 micromol/L (45-90); lamotrigine level well below her pre pregnancy value

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase the lamotrigine dose after checking the serum level
options.rationale: Normal platelets, transaminases, creatinine and protein excretion make pre eclampsia untenable, and a subtherapeutic level in a known epileptic reflects the pregnancy related rise in lamotrigine clearance that is corrected by dose escalation (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in Pregnancy; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in Pregnancy
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Give a magnesium sulfate loading dose and plan urgent birth today
options.rationale: Magnesium and expedited birth are the correct reflex when eclampsia is possible, but the blood pressure rise here is explained by the seizure itself and every biochemical marker of pre eclampsia is normal (Source: RANZCOG: Pre eclampsia and Hypertension in Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pre eclampsia and Hypertension in Pregnancy

options.text: Give intravenous labetalol and repeat the protein creatinine ratio
options.rationale: Intravenous therapy is used for a systolic of 160 mmHg or above or a diastolic of 110 mmHg or above, and a transient postictal reading of 148 over 94 does not meet that threshold (Source: RANZCOG: Pre eclampsia and Hypertension in Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Pre eclampsia and Hypertension in Pregnancy

options.text: Load with intravenous levetiracetam and admit her for observation
options.rationale: Acute loading with a second agent is for status epilepticus or repeated seizures, and adding polytherapy when the existing drug is simply underdosed is unnecessary (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Arrange urgent computed tomography of the brain before any treatment
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is indicated for a first ever seizure, focal features or failure to recover consciousness, and none of these applies to a known epileptic who has recovered fully (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: A seizure in the second half of pregnancy forces a rapid decision between eclampsia and an epileptic seizure, and getting it wrong in either direction is harmful. The discriminators are the biochemical and haematological markers of pre eclampsia together with the woman's own history, since a transient rise in blood pressure follows any generalised seizure. Lamotrigine is the specific trap in pregnancy because oestrogen induced glucuronidation increases its clearance so much that levels can fall by more than half by the third trimester, and breakthrough seizures cluster in women whose dose was never adjusted. Where genuine doubt remains, magnesium is given because the cost of treating an epileptic seizure with magnesium is far lower than the cost of missing eclampsia.
key_points: Normal platelets, liver enzymes, creatinine and protein excretion argue strongly against eclampsia
Blood pressure rises transiently after any generalised seizure
Lamotrigine clearance rises markedly through pregnancy and levels fall
Neuroimaging is for a first seizure, focal features or failure to recover
Treat as eclampsia when genuine diagnostic doubt persists
explanation.pearls: Reduce the lamotrigine dose back toward the pre pregnancy level within the first few days after birth, because clearance normalises rapidly and women left on the escalated third trimester dose develop ataxia, diplopia and rash within a fortnight.

subtopic_detail: Fertility sparing surgery for a suspected ovarian germ cell tumour
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar admitting a 19 year old university student with three weeks of increasing abdominal swelling and a dragging discomfort in her right side. She has felt her jeans getting tight and has been short of breath lying flat.

She has regular periods, has never been pregnant and takes no medication. There is a firm non tender mass arising from the pelvis reaching the umbilicus. Imaging shows a 14 cm solid right adnexal mass with areas of calcification, a normal left ovary and no ascites or peritoneal deposits. Her tumour markers have returned and computed tomography of the chest and abdomen shows no metastatic disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92, blood pressure 114/70, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Firm mobile pelvic mass reaching the umbilicus, no ascites, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Alpha fetoprotein 890 kIU/L (less than 10); lactate dehydrogenase 520 U/L (120-250); beta human chorionic gonadotrophin less than 2 IU/L; CA125 88 kU/L (less than 35); computed tomography shows no metastatic disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management?

options.text: Perform total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo oophorectomy
options.rationale: Radical surgery is the approach for advanced epithelial cancer in older women and would needlessly sterilise a 19 year old with disease confined to one ovary (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Give three cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy before any surgery
options.rationale: Neoadjuvant treatment is used for advanced epithelial disease that cannot be optimally debulked, whereas germ cell tumours are resected first and chemotherapy follows according to stage (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines

options.text: Arrange ultrasound guided biopsy of the mass before any surgery
options.rationale: Percutaneous biopsy of an ovarian mass risks tumour spill and capsule rupture, and the marker profile with imaging already provides the working diagnosis (Source: RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass

options.text: Perform fertility sparing unilateral salpingo oophorectomy with staging
options.rationale: A raised alpha fetoprotein with a solid unilateral mass in a young woman indicates a malignant germ cell tumour, which is highly chemosensitive, so removing the affected adnexa with surgical staging preserves fertility without compromising cure (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines; RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines
RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass

options.text: Observe with repeat imaging and tumour markers in eight weeks time
options.rationale: Observation is reasonable for a simple cyst under 5 cm, and a 14 cm solid mass with a markedly raised alpha fetoprotein requires operative management without delay (Source: RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass

explanation.summary: Ovarian malignancy in adolescence and young adulthood is dominated by germ cell tumours rather than the epithelial cancers of later life, and the treatment principles differ accordingly. Tumour markers point to histology before any tissue is obtained, with alpha fetoprotein indicating yolk sac elements, beta human chorionic gonadotrophin indicating choriocarcinoma and lactate dehydrogenase associated with dysgerminoma. These tumours are exquisitely sensitive to platinum based chemotherapy and cure rates exceed ninety per cent even with advanced disease, which is precisely why fertility preserving surgery is safe. Preserving the uterus and contralateral ovary allows most survivors to conceive naturally, and fertility preservation counselling before chemotherapy is standard.
key_points: Germ cell tumours predominate in women under 30 with an ovarian malignancy
Alpha fetoprotein indicates yolk sac elements and lactate dehydrogenase suggests dysgerminoma
Fertility sparing unilateral salpingo oophorectomy with staging is the standard operation
These tumours are highly chemosensitive with cure rates above ninety per cent
Percutaneous biopsy risks tumour spill and is avoided
explanation.pearls: Order alpha fetoprotein, beta human chorionic gonadotrophin and lactate dehydrogenase in any woman under 30 with a solid ovarian mass, because a mildly raised CA125 is common in this group and on its own misdirects toward an epithelial diagnosis.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Ovarian Cancer Guidelines
RANZCOG: Management of the Adnexal Mass

subtopic_detail: Biochemical thyrotoxicosis with hyperemesis in the first trimester
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar admitting a 26 year old woman at 9 weeks gestation who has been vomiting up to eight times a day for three weeks and has lost 5 kg. She cannot keep fluids down and feels dizzy on standing.

She has no previous thyroid disease and no family history of it. She has no neck swelling, no gritty or protruding eyes, no pretibial skin change and no tremor of the outstretched hands. Her thyroid function and antibody results have just returned. Her ultrasound confirms a single live intrauterine pregnancy with a crown rump length consistent with dates.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116, blood pressure 98/60, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, no goitre, no lid lag or proptosis, no tremor, no pretibial myxoedema
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); free thyroxine 28 pmol/L (10-20); thyroid stimulating hormone receptor antibodies not detected; potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2); ketones present on urinalysis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her thyroid results?

options.text: Start propylthiouracil at a low dose and review her in two weeks
options.rationale: Antithyroid drugs are reserved for true Graves disease in pregnancy and would risk maternal and foetal hypothyroidism in a condition that resolves spontaneously (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

options.text: Treat the vomiting supportively and recheck thyroid function later
options.rationale: Absent receptor antibodies with no goitre or eye signs indicate gestational transient thyrotoxicosis driven by chorionic gonadotrophin cross stimulation, which settles as levels fall and needs only rehydration, antiemetics and repeat testing by around 20 weeks (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy; RANZCOG: Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum

options.text: Start carbimazole and refer to endocrinology within one week
options.rationale: Carbimazole is additionally avoided in the first trimester because of an association with aplasia cutis and choanal atresia, and there is no indication for antithyroid therapy here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Arrange a technetium thyroid uptake scan to clarify the cause
options.rationale: Radionuclide uptake scanning is contraindicated in pregnancy, and the antibody result has already answered the question the scan would address (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Start propranolol and plan definitive treatment after the birth
options.rationale: Beta blockade may briefly relieve severe symptoms but she has no tremor or thyrotoxic symptoms independent of dehydration, and planning definitive therapy presumes a diagnosis that has been excluded (Source: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Human chorionic gonadotrophin shares a common alpha subunit with thyroid stimulating hormone and weakly stimulates the thyroid receptor, so a suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone in the first trimester is common and usually physiological. Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis sits at the severe end of that spectrum, correlates with the degree of vomiting, and is most marked around 9 to 11 weeks when gonadotrophin levels peak. The distinction from Graves disease rests on the absence of a goitre, orbitopathy, pretibial change and receptor antibodies, along with no preceding history of thyroid symptoms. Treating this condition with antithyroid drugs exposes mother and foetus to unnecessary risk for a process that resolves on its own by the middle of the second trimester.
key_points: Chorionic gonadotrophin cross stimulates the thyroid receptor in early pregnancy
Gestational transient thyrotoxicosis tracks with the severity of vomiting
Absent receptor antibodies with no goitre or eye signs exclude Graves disease
Management is rehydration, antiemetics and repeat thyroid function testing
Radionuclide scanning is contraindicated in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: A markedly raised free triiodothyronine with a free thyroxine only just above range points to Graves disease rather than gestational thyrotoxicosis, because the autoimmune process preferentially drives triiodothyronine secretion.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Thyroid Disease in Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Nausea and Vomiting of Pregnancy and Hyperemesis Gravidarum
Australian Medicines Handbook
